The problem asks for the maximum number of colors in a $45 \times 45 \times 45$ cube such that the set of colors in any $45 \times 45 \times 1$ prism in one orientation (say $xy$-plane) is the same as the set of colors in any $45 \times 45 \times 1$ prism in the other two orientations ($yz$-plane and $xz$-plane).

Let $S$ be the set of colors in any $45 \times 45 \times 1$ prism. Since there are 3 orientations and all prisms of a given orientation must have the same set of colors, let $C$ be the set of all colors used in the cube.
Let $R_i$ be the set of colors in the $i$-th "slice" perpendicular to the $x$-axis.
Let $C_j$ be the set of colors in the $j$-th "slice" perpendicular to the $y$-axis.
Let $L_k$ be the set of colors in the $k$-th "slice" perpendicular to the $z$-axis.
The condition states that for all $i, j, k \in \{1, \dots, 45\}$, the sets $R_i, C_j, L_k$ are all equal to the same set $S$.
This implies that every color $c \in C$ must appear in every slice $R_i$, every slice $C_j$, and every slice $L_k$.
Furthermore, since each unit cube $(x, y, z)$ belongs to exactly one $R_x$, one $C_y$, and one $L_z$, we must consider the distribution of colors.
Let $n_c$ be the number of unit cubes of color $c$.
If a color $c$ exists, it must appear at least once in every slice $R_1, \dots, R_{45}$. Since the slices $R_i$ are disjoint, $n_c \ge 45$.
Similarly, $c$ must appear in every slice $C_j$, so $n_c \ge 45$.
And $c$ must appear in every slice $L_k$, so $n_c \ge 45$.
However, the condition is stronger: the set of colors in *any* $45 \times 45 \times 1$ prism in *one* orientation must be the *same set* as the colors in *any* prism in the *other* orientations. 
Let $S$ be this set of colors, and let $|S| = k$.
For each color $c \in S$, let $X_c$ be the set of positions $(x, y, z)$ such that the cube at that position has color $c$.
The condition "the set of colors in any $45 \times 45 \times 1$ prism in the $xy$-plane is $S$" means that for every $z \in \{1, \dots, 45\}$, the set of colors $\{ \text{color}(x, y, z) : 1 \le x, y \le 45 \}$ is $S$.
This means every color $c \in S$ must appear at least once in every $z$-slice.
Similarly, every color $c \in S$ must appear at least once in every $y$-slice and every $x$-slice.
The total number of cubes is $45^3 = 91125$.
Let $c$ be a color. Let $I_c \subseteq \{1, \dots, 45\}^3$ be the positions of color $c$.
The condition that $c$ appears in every $z$-slice means that for every $z$, there is some $(x, y)$ such that $(x, y, z) \in I_c$.
The total number of colors is $k = |S|$.
Since each cube has exactly one color, the sets $I_c$ are disjoint.
Thus, $\sum_{c \in S} |I_c| \le 45^3$.
Since $c$ must appear in every $z$-slice, $|I_c| \ge 45$.
This gives $k \cdot 45 \le 45^3$, so $k \le 45^2 = 2025$.
Can we achieve $k=2025$?
If $k=2025$, each color $c$ must appear in exactly 45 positions, and these 45 positions must have distinct $x$-coordinates, distinct $y$-coordinates, and distinct $z$-coordinates (to satisfy the condition for all 3 orientations).
This is equivalent to partitioning the $45 \times 45 \times 45$ cube into 2025 Latin Squares of size $45 \times 45 \times 45$ or, more simply, a 3D permutation array.
Specifically, we want to assign a color $c \in \{1, \dots, 2025\}$ to each $(x, y, z)$ such that for every $c$, the coordinates of the cells with color $c$ form a permutation of $\{1, \dots, 45\}$ in each dimension.
